newsitem.title: CUBA: FEATURE - Tourism changes the landscape in Cuban resort.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tourism changes the landscape in Cuban resort.

text.p: Tourism is changing the landscape at the Cuban beach resort of Varadero as construction workers, cranes and tractors race to keep up with growing demand in a sector viewed as vital to Cuba's economic recovery.

So far there is little sign that the 10-month-old U.S. Helms-Burton law, designed to discourage foreign investment in Cuba, has had any effect on foreign firms involved in tourism, or on visitor numbers.

There is an air of muddy chaos behind Varadero's long beach, where several hotels are under construction, a new shopping centre is being completed and man-made lagoons dot what will be the resort's first full 18-hole golf course.
"This has the potential to be like Cancun (in Mexico)," said Pablo Morillas, representive in Varadero of Cubanacan SA, Cuba's largest state hotel chain.

Morillas, speaking during a trip last month to explain development in Varadero to foreign journalists, said the 22 km (13-mile) Varadero peninsula could eventually be the site for some 23,000-25,000 hotel rooms, compared with its current 8,000.

The town, 125 km (80 miles) east of Havana, heads Cuba's overall plan to double its current capacity of around 25,000 hotel rooms and regain its status as a leading Caribbean destination, a position lost after the 1959 revolution that brought President Fidel Castro to power.
GROWING TOURISM A MAJOR FOREIGN EXCHANGE EARNER

Tourism has been growing rapidly in recent years and the communist-ruled island expects at least 900,000 foreign visitors in 1996, up from 740,000 last year. Gross earnings from the sector in 1995 were $1 billion, with net profts estimated by authorities at about one third of that, making tourism a leading foreign exchange earner for Cuba.

Authorities say 1,800 new rooms will have been completed in Varadero in 1996, and the plan is to continue building at a rate of some 1,300-1,800 rooms a year. Vice-president Carlos Lage has called for more efficiency, saying construction delays cost tourist revenue.

The hurry is illustrated by Cubanacan's 331-room Gran Hotel, where builders are racing to meet a mid-November deadline for opening. In a sign of changing times in Cuba, the hotel is on the site of an old vacation centre for young Pioneers, Cuba's answer to the Boy Scouts.
Much of the building is still a skeleton. But hotel officials insisted it would be ready for the winter season that attracts a flood of visitors from Canada, Italy, Germany and Spain.

Although the Gran Hotel will be 100 percent Cuban-owned and managed, this is becoming a rarity. Half of Cubanacan's 54 hotels, which account for almost half Cuba's hotel rooms, are either foreign managed or joint owned.

Cubanacan deputy director Mario Sori enthused about the foreign input of management knowledge and sales and marketing from joint ventures that have blossomed since the first deals were signed in 1990.
The most obvious effect of the foreign input at the customer end has been a big improvement in the quality of food and service, say foreign hoteliers.

Cubanacan and other state hotel groups such as Gran Caribe and the military-owned Gaviota have ventures with firms such as Tryp, Sol Melia, Riu and Iberostar from Spain, Superclubs from Jamaica, Delta and Commonwealth Hospitality from Canada, Accor and Club Mediterranee from France, Going from Italy, LTI from Germany and Golden Tulip from the Netherlands.

The Helms-Burton law, passed in March and which includes provisions to punish foreign firms "trafficking" in nationalised property formerly owned by Americans, appears to have had no effect on existing investors in tourism.

Sol Melia, which manages three hotels in Varadero, one in Havana and two in eastern Cuba, is opening a new hotel in Varadero and launching a cruise ship in November, and has begun building a new hotel in Havana.

"We have had spectacular growth here in Cuba in the last six years," said Carlos Martinez, general manager of the Melia Varadero hotel. Sol Melia says it has been assured by the U.S. State Department that it will not be subject to penalties under Helms-Burton.

Eric Peyre, manager of one of LTI's four hotels in Cuba, the Tuxpan, also said his group planned to expand, adding Helms-Burton appeared to have had no effect on tourist numbers. Occupancy at the Tuxpan was expected to be slightly down this year but this was because the hotel raised prices, Peyre said.

Deals signed in the sector since Helms-Burton include a project with a Canadian entrepreneur to develop Jibacoa, an almost undeveloped beach about 60 km (40 miles) east of Havana and at least two new mangement deals with Italian firms.
